newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Sugar price rise seen possible from cyclone.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Sugar price rise seen possible from cyclone.

text.p: Significant damage to Australia's sugarcane crop over the weekend by cyclone Justin had industry growers and traders looking for a possible sugar price spike when New York and London markets re-opened.

Opinions were divided on whether sugar's long-depressed world price would be sparked into a rally by Justin's weekend flattening of sugarcane across widespread areas of the main cane-growing district of northeast Queensland.
Phil Lindsay of Ord Minnett Jardine Fleming Futures said a price spike to 13 U.S. cents a lb from Friday's New York close of 10.8 cents was possible.
"(But) if it's as bad as they're saying, 13 cents is highly likely and possibly 20 cents is also on the cards," he said.
At least 20 percent of Australia's once-expected 38-40 million tonnes of 1997/98 sugarcane had been seriously hit by Justin, Ian Ballantyne, general manager of CANEGROWERS, said.

The ultimate effect on Australian raw sugar production, while presently unknown, would be "pretty significant", he said. Queensland Sugar Corp (QSC) chief executive David Rutledge said after addressing an industry conference in Brisbane on Monday that cyclone damage to the current crop would need to be very extensive for it to affect world prices.
QSC's marketing manager Tom McNeill said sugar was a volatile and unpredictable market and price effects would ultimately come down to the extent of the damage.
But world stocks were high and significant price effects were not expected, he said. Rutledge earlier told the conference he saw static world sugar prices in 1997.

However in recent weeks, as Justin hovered off the Queensland coast, brokers and industry sources warned that substantial damage to Queensland's sugar crop might cause the international sugar price to spike.
Prices would not rise to 20 cents a lb even if Queensland's entire crop were wiped out, QSC's deputy chief executive Michael Bosscher recently said.
But broker Lindsay said: "I think we'll probably see a knee-jerk in New York and London but follow-on results with actual damage will be a couple of weeks away."
Sugar had not seen a bull market since 1979-1980. "This will be definitely a major impact," Lindsay said.
Justin, the first cyclone to seriously hit Australia's sugarcane crop since the 1970s, landed as Australia was in the final months before the cane crush began in June.
Australia produced 5.32 million tonnes of 94 net titre raw sugar last season and before cyclone Justin hit, was expected to produce a new record of 5.45 million tonnes for 1997/98.
Australia ranks about equal with Thailand and Brazil as the world's leading sugar exporters, with 1996/97 exports forecast at 4.25 million tonnes from 5.32 million tonnes production.
